title: Merge validation and cardinality
summary: Use merge validation to turn expected join cardinality into an executable assertion.

blocks.text: Use merge validation to turn expected join cardinality into an executable assertion.

items: validate="one_to_one" and similar modes catch accidental duplication.
Check the merge indicator when you need to audit unmatched keys.
Do not silently deduplicate keys unless the business rule defines which row to retain.

blocks.code: joined = left.merge(right, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one", indicator=True)
blocks.title: Example

rows: keys are unique in left and right
joining two tables at the same grain
expanding a dimension to its facts
enriching facts with a dimension (keeps the left grain)
only when row multiplication is intended

blocks.title: Worked example: pass, then fail loudly
blocks.code:
import pandas as pd

orders = pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1, 2, 3], "customer_id": [10, 10, 20]})
customers = pd.DataFrame({"customer_id": [10, 20, 30], "country": ["NO", "CH", "NO"]})

joined = orders.merge(customers, on="customer_id", how="left",
                      validate="many_to_one", indicator=True)
print(len(orders), len(joined))            # 3 3: the order grain is kept
print(joined["_merge"].value_counts())     # all "both": no unmatched orders

duplicated = pd.concat([customers, customers.iloc[[0]]])  # customer 10 twice
try:
    orders.merge(duplicated, on="customer_id", how="left", validate="many_to_one")
except pd.errors.MergeError as err:
    print("cardinality violated:", err)
blocks.explanation: validate checks key uniqueness only. It does not report unmatched keys (use indicator=True) and does not fix dtype mismatches. Bounded toy data; not executed during preparation.

blocks.title: SQL has no validate argument
blocks.text: In SQL, run the duplicate-key query from the grain step on the side that must be unique, or compare COUNT(*) before and after the join. An unexpected increase is fan-out.
